description: How substances move into, out of and around the human body. Key concepts and applications explained.
content_html:
Diffusion

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration — down a concentration gradient. Diffusion is passive: it requires no energy input from the cell. The particles move by random motion until they are evenly spread.

The rate of diffusion is increased by:

  • A steeper concentration gradient (larger difference in concentration across a surface)
  • A larger surface area
  • A thinner membrane (shorter diffusion distance)
  • A higher temperature (particles move faster)
Key Fact

Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient — from high to low concentration. It is passive (no energy needed). Rate increases with steeper gradient, larger surface area, thinner membrane and higher temperature.

Osmosis

Osmosis is a special case of diffusion involving water. Water molecules move from a region of higher water potential (a more dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (a more concentrated solution) through a partially permeable membrane. Like diffusion, osmosis is passive and requires no energy.

Osmosis is vital for cells: if the fluid surrounding a cell is more dilute than the cell contents, water moves into the cell by osmosis — the cell swells. If the surrounding fluid is more concentrated, water moves out and the cell shrinks. Red blood cells and plant cells are particularly affected by changes in the water concentration of their environment.

Plant cells placed in a very dilute solution gain water by osmosis and become turgid — the vacuole expands and pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall, making the cell firm. This turgor pressure is what keeps plant stems and leaves rigid. In a concentrated solution, plant cells lose water, the vacuole shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall — the cell is said to be plasmolysed.

Animal cells, which have no cell wall, are more vulnerable to osmotic damage. A red blood cell placed in a very dilute solution will take in water until it bursts (lysis). In a concentrated solution it will shrink and become crenated (shrivelled). This is why intravenous fluids given in hospitals are carefully formulated to match the salt concentration of blood plasma.

Active Transport

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. This requires energy from respiration and uses carrier proteins embedded in the cell membrane. Active transport is essential when cells need to absorb substances that are already present in higher concentration inside the cell.

Examples include: absorption of glucose from the small intestine into blood (when glucose concentration is already higher in the blood); uptake of mineral ions by root hair cells from soil (soil solution contains very low concentrations of minerals).

The Circulatory System

Humans have a double circulation: the blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body — once through the lungs (pulmonary circuit) to pick up oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, and once through the body (systemic circuit) to deliver oxygen and nutrients to tissues. This allows mammals to maintain high blood pressure in both circuits and sustain the high metabolic rates needed for warm-blooded activity.

Key Fact

The human circulatory system is a double circulation: blood travels from the heart to the lungs (pulmonary circuit) and separately from the heart to the body (systemic circuit). The heart is the pump that drives both circuits.

Gas Exchange in the Alveoli

The lungs are adapted for efficient gas exchange through millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. The alveoli have several adaptations that maximise the rate of diffusion:

  • Very large surface area — millions of alveoli provide an enormous total surface area.
  • Very thin walls — one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is minimal.
  • Rich blood supply — capillaries surrounding each alveolus continuously carry oxygenated blood away and deliver deoxygenated blood, maintaining steep concentration gradients for both oxygen and carbon dioxide.
  • Moist lining — gases must dissolve to cross cell membranes.

Blood Components and Their Functions

Blood is a tissue consisting of four main components, each transported around the body by the circulatory system:

  • Red blood cells — contain haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen in the lungs and releases it in body tissues. Their biconcave shape gives a large surface area for oxygen uptake, and their lack of nucleus maximises haemoglobin content.
  • White blood cells — part of the immune system. They engulf pathogens (phagocytes) or produce antibodies (lymphocytes) to defend the body against infection.
  • Platelets — small cell fragments that trigger blood clotting at a wound site, preventing excessive blood loss and forming a barrier to infection.
  • Plasma — the yellow liquid that carries red and white blood cells, platelets, dissolved glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide around the body.

All three processes move substances across membranes, but they differ in key ways:

  • Diffusion — passive, down concentration gradient, any small molecule.
  • Osmosis — passive, down water potential gradient, water only, through a partially permeable membrane.
  • Active transport — requires energy from respiration, against concentration gradient, uses carrier proteins, specific molecules.

A common error is describing active transport as “pumping substances both ways” — it moves substances specifically against the gradient, not simply in a random direction.
exam_tip_html: When explaining diffusion or osmosis in a biological context, always name the direction of movement relative to the concentration gradient and state whether energy is required. For alveoli adaptation questions, link each adaptation directly to a factor that increases diffusion rate — e.g. “thin walls reduce the diffusion distance, increasing the rate of gas exchange.” Describing active transport: you must mention the concentration gradient is reversed AND that energy from respiration is required.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Diffusion is the passive net movement of particles down a concentration gradient. Osmosis is the special case of diffusion involving water through a partially permeable membrane from high to low water potential.
  • Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient using energy from respiration and carrier proteins — essential for glucose absorption in the gut and mineral uptake in roots.
  • The human double circulatory system separates the pulmonary (lung) and systemic (body) circuits. The alveoli in the lungs are adapted for rapid gas exchange through large surface area, thin walls and a rich capillary blood supply.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes osmosis?
A) The movement of all molecules from high to low concentration using energy
B) The net movement of water from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
C) The movement of glucose against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins
D) The random movement of particles in all directions equally
practice_questions.marks: B) The net movement of water from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which active transport differs from diffusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following:
• Active transport requires energy (from respiration); diffusion does not [1 mark]
• Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient; diffusion moves with the gradient [1 mark]
• Active transport uses carrier proteins in the membrane; diffusion does not require carrier proteins [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the alveoli are adapted to maximise the rate of gas exchange.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Large surface area provided by millions of alveoli [1 mark]; walls only one cell thick, minimising diffusion distance [1 mark]; rich capillary blood supply continuously removes oxygen and delivers carbon dioxide, maintaining steep concentration gradients [1 mark]; moist lining allows gases to dissolve before diffusing across the membrane [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four adaptations, each linked to diffusion rate.
Developing: One or two adaptations named without mechanistic link to diffusion.
Emerging: Vague reference to lungs being good at gas exchange.

practice_questions.text:
A student places a piece of potato in a concentrated salt solution and a second piece in pure water. After 30 minutes, the potato in salt solution has decreased in mass and the potato in water has increased in mass.
Explain these results using your knowledge of osmosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The salt solution is more concentrated than the potato cell contents [1 mark]; water moves out of the potato cells by osmosis (down the water potential gradient) into the salt solution [1 mark]; cells lose water, causing the potato to decrease in mass [1 mark]. In water, the solution is more dilute than the cell contents; water moves into the potato cells by osmosis, increasing their mass [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four points.
Developing: Correct direction for one condition, without explanation in terms of water potential.
Emerging: States water moves in or out without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain why root hair cells require active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil, whereas oxygen moves into blood by diffusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mineral ions are present in very low concentrations in the soil but in higher concentration inside the root hair cell [1 mark]; so minerals must be moved against the concentration gradient, which requires energy from respiration via active transport [1 mark]; oxygen, by contrast, is at higher concentration in the alveoli than in the blood, so it can move down its gradient by diffusion without energy [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three points.
Developing: States active transport requires energy without connecting to concentration gradient comparison.
Emerging: Names both processes but does not explain the distinction.

practice_questions.text: Explain the advantages of the double circulatory system over a single circulatory system in meeting the high metabolic demands of mammals.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit [1 mark]; the pulmonary circuit (heart to lungs) replenishes oxygen and removes CO₂ [1 mark]; the systemic circuit (heart to body) delivers oxygenated blood at high pressure to all tissues [1 mark]; separating the two circuits means blood is re-pressurised after passing through the lungs, so it reaches tissues at high pressure [1 mark]; high pressure means faster delivery of oxygen and glucose to active cells, sustaining high metabolic rates [1 mark]; a single circulation would have low pressure reaching the body after passing through the lungs, insufficient for active mammals [1 mark].
Secure: Four or five points clearly explained.
Developing: Describes the two circuits without explaining the pressure advantage.
Emerging: States blood goes to the lungs and body.

knowledge_checks.q: Which process moves substances against the concentration gradient and requires energy from respiration?
What type of circulation do humans have?
The alveoli have _____ walls (one cell thick) to minimise the distance that oxygen must diffuse.
In osmosis, water moves from a region of _____ water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
Match each transport process to its key feature:
right: Passive; net movement of particles down concentration gradient
Passive; water only; through a partially permeable membrane
Requires energy; moves substances against concentration gradient

flashcard_questions.a: Net movement of particles from high to low concentration (down the gradient); passive, no energy needed.

flashcard_questions.q: How does increasing surface area affect diffusion rate?
flashcard_questions.a: It increases the rate — more surface area means more molecules can cross at the same time.
The net movement of water from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to a plant cell placed in a concentrated solution?
flashcard_questions.a: It loses water by osmosis, the vacuole shrinks, and the cell becomes plasmolysed.

flashcard_questions.q: What energy source does active transport use?
Give one example of active transport in the human body.
flashcard_questions.a: Absorption of glucose from the small intestine into blood when blood glucose is already higher.

flashcard_questions.q: What is meant by the double circulatory system?
flashcard_questions.a: Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: once to the lungs and once to the body.

flashcard_questions.q: Name four adaptations of the alveoli for gas exchange.
flashcard_questions.a: Large surface area, thin walls (one cell thick), rich capillary blood supply, moist lining.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do root hair cells use active transport to absorb minerals?
flashcard_questions.a: Mineral concentration in the soil is lower than inside the cell, so energy is needed to move them against the gradient.

glossary_terms.definition: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, by random motion. No energy is required.

The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential (more dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (more concentrated solution) through a partially permeable membrane.
A membrane that allows small molecules such as water to pass through but blocks larger molecules.

The movement of substances from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration — against the concentration gradient — using energy from respiration and carrier proteins in the membrane.

A circulatory system in which blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: once to collect oxygen from the lungs (pulmonary circuit) and once to deliver it to the body tissues (systemic circuit).
Tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange between air and blood takes place by diffusion. They are adapted with a large surface area, thin walls and a rich blood supply.
Biconcave disc-shaped cells in blood that contain haemoglobin and carry oxygen from the lungs to respiring tissues. They have no nucleus to maximise space for haemoglobin.
The red protein in red blood cells that binds reversibly to oxygen in the lungs and releases it in respiring tissues.
